builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
summary: The framework replaces informal token accounting with a thermodynamic decomposition of agent cost into work and heat, using coding/uncoding cycles and test suites as the evaluator. It costs only instrumentation of existing agent runs (token counting per model call and repeated cycle experiments), with no model changes, but applying the Jarzynski-style estimation requires many repeated runs that themselves consume tokens. Its conclusions can fail to transfer because the measured ratios depend on the specific agent, model, sampling temperature, and test-suite reliability, and the paper notes that imperfect test suites can accept broken changes, corrupting the work/heat accounting.
rationale: The paper offers a measurement framework and empirical findings about token waste in coding agents, not a deployable optimization method, so it informs cost-awareness but does not yield an implementable gain today.
technique: Thermodynamic accounting of agent token cost

claims.statement: The framework replaces informal token accounting with a thermodynamic decomposition of agent cost into work and heat, using coding/uncoding cycles and test suites as the evaluator. It costs only instrumentation of existing agent runs (token counting per model call and repeated cycle experiments), with no model changes, but applying the Jarzynski-style estimation requires many repeated runs that themselves consume tokens. Its conclusions can fail to transfer because the measured ratios depend on the specific agent, model, sampling temperature, and test-suite reliability, and the paper notes that imperfect test suites can accept broken changes, corrupting the work/heat accounting.

About 80% of tokens in successful runs are generated in calls that leave the requested change unchanged ('heat'); estimated free energy is 14-22% of mean successful-run cost; coding costs 1.1-1.5x uncoding. These are measurements, not an improvement factor.
